title: Brothers by nature
hook: don't be harsh with your slave; he's your brother, born of the same Zeus (Discourses 1.13)
carry: look where your eyes are pointed

segments.voice: Yesterday: content with what comes, and your line, content. Which unchosen thing did you try wanting, just as it was? Day three hundred ninety-nine, the end of the week.

The coffee comes out lukewarm. The order is wrong. The person at the counter didn't hear you the first time. It's amazing how fast a calm, kind person can turn sharp at someone whose job is to serve them. A student asked Epictetus something that sounds almost silly: how can I eat dinner in a way that pleases the gods? His answer went straight to the person bringing the hot water. Today: adelphos.
screen: `THE COFFEE COMES OUT LUKEWARM.` → `HOW DO I EAT TO PLEASE THE GODS?` → `LOOK AT WHO BRINGS THE WATER.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book one, chapter thirteen. Eat justly, Epictetus says, with gratitude, with moderation and good order, and you've eaten in a way the gods accept. Then he gets concrete. You call for warm water, and the slave doesn't hear. Or he brings it lukewarm. Or he isn't in the house at all. Not to rage, not to explode: that is acceptable to the gods. But how am I supposed to put up with someone like that? And here Epictetus turns sharp. Won't you bear with your own brother, he asks, who has Zeus as his ancestor, born from the same seed as you? You're not his owner first. You're his kin. The student pushes back: but I bought him. He didn't buy me. And Epictetus says: look where your eyes are pointed. Down at the dirt, at the laws of dead men. You're not looking at the laws of the gods. We should hear this with open eyes. Epictetus had been a slave himself before he was freed. Yet this chapter doesn't call for slavery to end. It asks owners for gentleness, not freedom. But the root of the idea is bigger than its century: whoever hands you the cup is your brother or sister by nature. Look back at the week: kin, not more books, it fits, look closer, love stays, content. And today, adelphos.
screen: `EAT JUSTLY, WITH GRATITUDE.` · `THE LUKEWARM WATER.` · `YOUR BROTHER, FROM THE SAME SEED.` · `READ IT WITH OPEN EYES.` · then, large: `BROTHERS BY NATURE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and breathe. Bring to mind the people who served you this week: a cashier, a driver, a nurse, a cleaner, someone on a customer service line. Picture one face, even if you barely saw it. Let yourself see them as kin, someone with a family, a tired back, a whole life. If you were short with anyone, notice it without beating yourself up. Then decide on one gentle thing you'll say to the next person who serves you. The bell holds the time.
Adelphos. Greek for brother, literally 'from the same womb': Epictetus' word for the one who serves you, your kin before anything else.
Your line: look where your eyes are pointed. Today, be gentle with someone who serves you, especially if they get something wrong. Day three hundred ninety-nine, and a week done.

howItsDone: Some readers of Epictetus apply this chapter to how they treat people who serve them, such as waiters, cleaners and call-center staff, especially when something goes wrong.

fork.setup: you're a Roman master. you asked for warm water and the slave brought it lukewarm. what does Epictetus say?
options: punish him so it doesn't happen again.
bear with your brother; he comes from the same seed as you.
fork.reveal: he calls the servant the master's brother by nature, and says looking only at 'I bought him' is looking at the laws of dead men.

original.note: Greek adelphos: brother, literally 'from the same womb'; Epictetus uses it for the master's kinship with the slave.

trapdoor: what you thought: be polite to staff.
what it means: the one who serves you is your kin by nature, not a lesser kind of person.
what a scholar hears: Epictetus, a former slave, grounds this in shared descent from Zeus, yet the chapter asks masters for gentleness rather than an end to slavery, a tension some readers note.
recall: the senator who kept going in

Epictetus' enslavement: owned by Epaphroditus, a freedman and secretary of Nero; later freed. Confirm phrasing.
